Feb 1996   No.103   Page Reply

 How to write to us...02     -

 John Legros..........03    04

 Herbert Smart........08    12

 Ken Jones............14    21

 Bernadette Dowsland..24    27

 Fred Ridout..........31    33

 Peter Johnson........35    48

 Chris Norfolk........49    50

   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From John Legros, BRUSSELS

Dear Ron,

Congratulations for OUTLET +D
and PC - they are wonderful!
I wonder if you can help me? I
have a couple of questions conc-
erning the Spectrum with +D...

1. What does the expression:
   SPECIAL FILE mean and how do
   you create one from BASIC?

2. What is an 'MD' file and how
   can one be created in BASIC?

3. How can you switch the IY
   machine code instruction from
   23610 to another address? And
   for unlimited duration?
                  -  John Legros

Brian Cavers to John Legros

The Disciple and +D SPECIAL file
type is generally intended for
commercial software producers. A
SPECIAL file cannot be directly
accessed from BASIC using LOAD
and SAVE. The intention is that
a commercial program would use
its own machine code routines to
read and write to the file thus
preventing the average user from
meddling with it. The file could
be anything - a picture, text,
program or whatever.

All files have a distinct number
in the disk CAT to denote their
type. A SPECIAL file is 8 so any
file could be altered to a SPEC-
IAL type by using SAVE @ to
change the disk CAT.

The following will change the
first file in the CAT to a SPEC-
IAL file...

11 LOAD @1,0,1,55555
22 POKE 55555,8     :REM CAT No.
33 SAVE @1,0,1,55555

It will then show as a SPECIAL
file in the CAT. The file will
still load as normal, eg,a BASIC
file changed to a SPECIAL in
this way can still load with
either LOAD P1 or LOAD d1;"NAME"

MD or M/DRIVE files will emulate
microdrive files of any type. I
think they were for access by
machine code programs that
directly access microdrives and
thus would work on Disciple or
*D. Their CAT code number is 6.

You should not change IY in a
machine code program if it calls
a ROM routine. If it doesn't and
you disable interrupts with DI
then there is no problem; you
simply stack IY and pop it back
after, eg...


DI
PUSH IY                ;store IY
LD IY,NNNN          ;any address
program....        ;your program
POP IY               ;restore IY
EI
RET


Alternatively you could forget
the PUSH and POP and just LD IY
with 23610 before exit.


When BASIC is running,IY must be
ALWAYS pointing at 23610 as the
offsets from that address are
system variables changed by the
ROM using IY. Thus in your own
machine code program you can
change IY permanently and leave
it running all day - it doesn't
matter. Only when you return to
BASIC or call the ROM (probably
SOME ROM routines are safe) is
it crucial to restore IY to
23610.

I am assuming its necessary to
disable interrupts - I've not
actually looked to see if the
key routines, etc. use IY.

                       Brian

From H. Smart, SELKIRK


Dear Brian,

Some time ago I wrote to you and
asked for some back numbers of
OUTLET on tape.  After receiving
several cassettes I had trouble
loading them and I stopped gett-
ing any more. I have now managed
to obtain a Plus D interface and
disk drive (secondhand) and I
would now like to get further
copies from you on Plus D disks.

My setup was a Spectrum Plus 2A
but now it is a Spectrum Plus 2
(without the "A"), a Plus D
interface and a three and a half
inch disk drive.


I have run into one or two snags
however and I was wondering if
you can help me! It is asking a
lot so if you charge for advice,
please let me know.

First, I did not know that the
Plus D interface will not work
with the Plus 2A Spectrum. I
think it has something to do
with the PSU - the Plus 2A has
both 12 volt and 5 volt supplies
and the Plus 2 has only the 9
volt supply but since I got the
Plus 2 in the deal I'm now using
that.

But there is another snag. My
printer is an old but still
working (as you can see!) New-
bury Data 1500 made by C. Itoh,
Inc.

My printer needs an RS232 (seri-
al) port and when the Plus D is
plugged in, it completely covers
up the RS232 port! which means I
can't use the Plus D at the same
time as the printer!


Then I found I could not get the
printer to work with the Spec-
trum Plus 2!  I can't find out
why.


The Tasword Plus 2 manual tells
me to enter line 60 RANDOMIZE
USR 40458: FORMAT "P";nnnn where
nnnn is the baud rate of the
printer. This I've tried but
the printer just prints out
garbage.


I can still use the Tasword with
my old Spectrum Plus 2A but it's
a bit of a bind having to keep
changing everything over. Well I
hope you can help me as I am an
OAP and don't want to have to
buy another printer (parallel
port).


       Yours faithfully,

           H. Smart


Brian Cavers to Herbert Smart

You should by now have received
Ron's reply and Datel's leaflet
indicating that the +D can be
got to work with the Plus 2A
with an extra gadget.

If you have no luck with them,
you might try Brian Gaff. Though
his business is no longer trad-
ing, Brian did tell me he had a
few bits and pieces left. His
address is:
           BRIAN GAFF
        64 ROEBUCK ROAD
          CHESSINGTON
             SURREY
            KT9 1JX

       TEL: 0181 287 4180


The gadget is called a FIXIT and
was priced at `9.50.

If you write to him then please
print or write with large clear
lettering as Brian is a regist-
ered blind person. Remember to
state that it is for a +2A and,
if inquiring, enclose an SAE.

It occurs to me that with the
FIXIT plugged in, you may have
room for the RS232 connection!

                       Brian

From Ken Jones, VARMO, ITALY




Dear Ron and Brian,

Thanks for yours of 1/11/95 re-
garding disk mail-shielding.

Of 19 disks received, two got
damaged;so I appear to be well
over the fraction of 1% norm
which other subscribers report.

It would have surprised no-one
were the damage caused by local,
Italian, post offices, whose
cavalier approach to the public
is a fact of life; but this time
they are blameless!


When disks were dispatched in
quite flimsy envelopes, you
state that the reject rate had
been no worse. The reason may
have been psychological. A date-
stamp basher might stay his hand
before a manifestly fragile ob-
ject but may pound on regardless
when confronted with a padded
envelope.


Be that as it may, I think we
agree that if the disks are in-
serted with the slider end down,
away from the stamp-stomping
area, the security of the oper-
ation is improved at no extra
cost except to you, Ron, who has
first to position each disk
properly.


Which brings me to a question. I
am in my 74th year to Heaven or,
in default, to some other Place.
A retired telecomms. production
engineer, I have worked in Italy
since 1953 for Italian, British
and Dutch masters.


Like the superannuated account-
ant who mentally adds up any
column of figures he sees (be
they even the departure times on
a railway schedule) my instinct
for asking people how they solve
certain operational problems
remains undiminished even
though, on occasion, it could
result in a bop on the nose! In
your case I'll chance it.



You must duplicate and dispatch
some hundreds of disks and other
forms of media per month. How do
you execute such a plethora of
formatting, copying and so on
while still leaving time to pro-
duce 'Outlet', let alone answer-
ing gormless questions such as
this?


Now please bear with me and lis-
ten again.


Outletters No. 19 discussed with
Mr. Pollard the problem of manu-
als. It is a vexed question,
particularily for those living
out in the sticks as I do.



Manuals come essentially in two
levels. Firstly,the Penfold/Kan-
taris type of spartan introduct-
ions to systems or programs.
Basically(no pun intended)they
are slim, low-priced volumes
which clearly can only go so
far. At the other end are the
tomes, costing more than some-
what, supplied by the great and
aimed at professional users who
don't have to pick up the bill
anyway - much like present-day
diplomacy where nothing exists
between pseudo-peace talks and
sending in the marines.

What little programming I do is
in QBasic.I have bought a small
book and I have an 'On Screen
Tutorial' which modestly styles


itself 'A Survival Guide to
QBasic'.At best it is moderately
useful,at worst it can be down-
right misleading.


An example: 'WAIT'. On my first
12k of Spectrum 'PAUSE' was
simple; 'WAIT'is beyond my
ken(pun intended).My little book
only cites it to warn that it is
a 'Reserved' word and not to be
made free with. The tutorial
tells me how to use it and then
crashes my program.


Certainly the fault is mine
alone, since others must surely
use QBasic and 'WAIT' daily with
careless abandon.


There is a book, 'QBasic for
Dummies' which costs around 18
GBpounds + postage and,to me,
exchange rates. This I would
readily pay were I sure that it
will teach this old dog some new
tricks.

Does anyone recommend it or
something like it?

My ref: D:LTR2.CZN

                   Ken Jones

Ron & Brian to Ken Jones

Some of this may tread ground
already covered but it is worth
re-stating: There are 4 categ-
ories of returns. 1) Damaged -
which you have suffered twice
and is, as you say, way above
the norm (we have many readers
that have received OUTLET every
month since Sep '87 without
returns of any kind).2) Corrupt-
who can tell when this happens,
samples are taken during dupli-
cation and test-loaded, we also
use (on the Plus D) what we call
the "leap-frog" method of copy-
ing where each copy is used to
produce the next copy:this means
that any corrupt files show up
at the duplication stage.


3) "Reported corrupt" but, in
fact, they always load perfectly
OK on our systems.

See also DRIVECHAT in this issue
about drive variations which may
account for this.

4) Our error. Occasionally a
blank disk or a wrong issue is
sent out (bet you can hardly
believe we make mistakes!). In
spite of all the care we take,
when you're duplicating on 3 or
4 different systems and maybe
typing in a letter on another,
it does happen - remembering
also that nothing is labelled at
that stage (what's the point of
labelling a disk that may be
discarded if it won't format or
duplicate).

All OUTLET disks are now sent
out in padded envelopes (which
cost us 5 to 6 times as much as
before) and they have, for some
time now, been inserted slider
end first so, we hope we have
laid problems with damaged disks
to rest although, again as we
have said before, short of pack-
ing the disks in steel there is
not much more we can do.

Your question how do we cope
with the various OUTLET jobs
needs an article to explain in
detail (one day, soon, perhaps)
but could be summarised as...

Organisation, constant develop-
ment and refinement of routines,
staying flexible enough to cope
with the unexpected.    R & B

From Bernadette Dowsland, GOOLE

Dear Ron,

I have used opentype files on
the +D and I know there are
routines in +3DOS as well but no
Basic to support them. I know
that Hisoft +3 Basic Compiler
implements them (pity I don't
have a copy) and also that
Mallard Basic does too (I took
one look at Mallard Basic when I
got it and haven't looked at it
since).

Can someone point me in the
right direction or come up with
some m/c routines to provide
extended Basic in 128 mode for
opentype files on the +3?


Now on the subject of the light-
gun. The disc with the +3 has 6
games, it also has a clever menu
that uses the lightgun to sel-
ect.Now the m/c routine involved
seems only to return a vertical
co-ordinate back into a Basic
variable to operate the menu.


Now if I was ever to attempt to
write a Basic game with the
lightgun (did I hear someone say
heaven forbid) then I would need
a horizontal variable agreed?

Well the games on the disc must
have the suitable machine code
but me being a m/c thicky would
never find it. Can anyone help
with this?


One more query, in the lightgun
game Bullesye, I tried to cheat
by finding the quiz questions
and answers using the Multiface
but no way.  Is there a clever
formula that m/c programmers can
employ in such quiz games in
order to condense ASCII code
down to less than 1 Byte per
letter to get more questions in
less memory?

         Yours faithfully,

        Bernadette Dowsland

Brian to Bernadette Dowsland

I've never heard of any BASIC
extension to +3 BASIC that lets
you open, read and write to
files which is a bit surprising
in a way. It would need quite a
bit of work but would be useful
to a lot of programmers. It may
be that anyone who had the idea
might have thought that Mallard
Basic does it so why bother but
not many people use Mallard. If
anyone has heard of such soft-
ware then please write in.

It might be worth examining the
lightgun machine code to see how
it extracts the vertical coordi-
nate - it 'might' be easy to do
a routine for the horizontal.


You can send in the code if you
like and I'll give it a quick
look - though I can't promise I
will find anything - and I don't
have a light gun anyway.

By the way, does the Basic use
the vertical variable directly
or does it use something like
INT(Y/256). The thought occurred
to me that it may be a double
byte which includes both vertic-
al and horizontal but that part-
icular Basic program only needed
the vertical component for the
menu.

Surely someone must have info on
how to use the lightgun. Anyone?
It must surely be provided for
programmers somehow.


Yes, there are numerous ways to
compress ASCII text - so many
that there is no standard way
and therefore no easy way to
read those quiz answers.

I had a similar problem very re-
cently on the PC. I was testing
a graphic adventure for our PC
OUTLET and quite enjoying it
when I got stuck. Nothing, abso-
lutely nothing I could think up
could get me any further.


I found a text file with, I'm
sure, a good chance of some
prompt or other that might give
me a clue but unfortunately it
was all garbage and clearly
condensed text.


Condensed text is effectively
like code and just as difficult
to crack so I gave up straight
away - I know there are just too
many ways to encode text (and in
this case as well as yours, the
text may be DELIBERATELY encoded
in a tricky way to make it al-
most impossible to crack!)

Apart from hacking the machine
code, it might be possible to
make a snaphot file using Multi-
face 3. Then unlock it with the
M3UNLOCK. This presumably makes
code files which might be loaded
separately and examined and the
text might be already decoded!

                         Brian

From Fred Ridout, SWINDON

Dear Ed's,

There are a couple of questions
I would like to ask.

Firstly, the command to access
the silicon disk on the +2 in
BASIC is ! while on the +3 it is
"m:". Is the command in machine
code the same for both?

Secondly, is there an Art Studio
specifically for the +3? I tried
the conversion on your latest
OUTLET but I'm afraid it is a
little beyond me.My effort gives
the error...

"Drive must be A: or B: , 50:1"


I used Version 2.0,128K Advanced
Art Studio.

All the best and keep up the
good work.

                    Fred

Brian Cavers to Fred Ridout

I don't think accessing the RAM
disk from machine code on a +3,
which uses +3 DOS, can be any-
thing like the same as a +2. If
you are looking a universal way
of using the RAM disk then I can
only suggest using SPECTEST from
OUTLET 83 to determine whether
the program is running on a +3
or otherwise and then running
different lines.Does anyone else
know any better?

I do not think there is a +3
version of Art Studio but just a
tape version. However, it does
look like you might have a diff-
erent tape version with another
drive address.


If I were you I would try the
whole conversion one more time.
Are there any user inputs and if
so, does it ask for the drive?
If so, does it need an "A:"input
or a 0. John Cleveland (see his
separate letter) succeeded with
the conversion so hopefully he
or Cristian Secara might be able
to offer some suggestions.

                       Brian.

From Peter Johnson, NEW ZEALAND


Greetings to you and the OUTLET
membership from NEW ZEALAND. It
has been some time since I last
contributed a letter. Although
some of my technical contribut-
ions have appeared over several
months, these were actually
written some time ago.

The following is a collection of
technical bits and pieces
relating to the Spectrum that I
have accumulated since the
original material was written.
Some of it come from matters
raised in the letters section
and some from additional
observation I have made.


What I have written about in the
past has been associated with
the 48K and the grey 128 +2
Spectrums. I am not able to
contribute anything on the +3 as
I do not have one nor any tech-
nical information on this model.
As far as I am aware there is
only one of this type in my
local area. A request - can
anyone supply me with a circuit
diagram or better still the
technical manual?

In one letter there was a comm-
ent that a green screen monitor
was of low resolution (poor
detail). I can assure the writer
of that comment that the green
screen monitor can be as sharp
as a black and white one.


When using the direct video sys-
tem, a green screen monitor is
much superior to a colour
receiver. This I can vouch for
as I have three green screens
monitors in regular use.

Since the material on the use of
direct video for monitors was
written  (see OUTLET 89,90) I
have been able to obtain some
RGB monitors. I knew that the
RGB feed to the monitor would
give a better picture display,
it fact the results were
excellent beyond expectations.
I was able to have two monitors
operating side by side for
comparison. One was fed with the
normal composite video, and the
other with the RGB feeds, this
was from a Spectrum 128 +2.

This A, B comparison immediately
showed the RGB monitor to be
superior in several ways. The
border, paper and coloured areas
were clean without any back-
ground grain, text is crisp and
clean without any colour fringes
and the colours are clean and
precise.


When one analyses the situation
it stands to reason that the
results would be better. Within
the computer the three colour
signals RED, BLUE  and GREEN
(RGB) are each generated separ-
ately: the monitor display tube
has three separate guns to acti-
vate the RED , BLUE and GREEN
dots on the screen.


It seems to be a pointless extr-
avagance to require a complex
integrated circuit within the
computer to mix (encode) the RGB
signals then within the monitor
to use equally complex circuit
to unmix (decode) these same
signals back again just to
enable them to be fed between
the computer and monitor via a
single short piece of coaxial
cable. The encoding and subse-
quent decoding involve a number
of compromises and as a result
the picture quality suffers.

The requirements for this
encoding process being used are
historical.When the Spectrum and
other similar computers were
originally produced a normal


domestic TV set was available
for the display and its input is
the encoded signal. This in turn
was the reqirement of the broad-
casting system since only one
transmitter is used to carry the
tv signal.

To give some variety to this
written material, load the TEST-
CARD program.


 [Press N to load it here now or
 C from the CONTENTS page - Ed]


This test chart has a number of
features which can be used to
check and if necessary adjust
your monitor/TV set...


1  The black squares around the
perimeter are true black, adjust
the BRIGHTNESS control to set
these to a true black and not a
grey.


2  The colour bars should all be
clearly defined, note that the
lower third of these is BRIGHT
which will show if this is
available. On a black and white
monitor, or if the colour can be
turned off, these colour bars
will show as a grey scale with
the right hand blue bar appear-
ing as a dark grey. The contrast
control should be adjusted so
each bar from left to right is a
decending order of brightness.



3  The background and border
should be a pure white without a
green or blue or red cast Inter-
nal adjustments within the moni-
tor are necessary to correct a
colour cast.


4  The resolution blocks across
the lower centre should be
clearly defined without colour
fringes. The righthand one is
individual pixels. These will
show clearly on a good quality
black and white/green monitor
but will not show on a colour
receiver even on direct video.
A high resolution colour monitor
will show these only on a RGB
input.



5   The cross hatch grid lines
should also be clearly defined
black lines. A red ,blue,or
yellow fringe on either side or
above or below the lines in one
or more parts of the display
indicates a possible convergence
error.This will require internal
adjustment of the colour monitor
or tv set to correct.

A blue or yellow outline on the
vertical lines and also on the
resolution blocks probably indi-
cates an encoding error, this
will only appear on a composite
video feed and not on RGB
inputs. Both my 128 +2 exhibit
this problem which I suspect is
a design defect.



6  Each colour block should
finish precisely and not tend to
tail off to the right.  Again,
this effect sould only appear on
a composite video feed and not
on RGB.The likely cause is the
same design defect as mentioned
in 5. Should it occur on an RGB
fed monitor the cause might be
poor performance of the monitor
video amplifiers or poor cable
driver systems within the
computor.


A test chart such as this can
give a good indication of how
well or otherwise your computer
display is performing. A lot
more could be said but I will
leave that for now.


The 48k Spectrum can be modified
to provide a a direct video feed
to a monitor, a video amplifier
to do this was described in an
earlier issue. (OUTLET 89 and
90) However as it stands it has
no facilities for RGB feeds. I
am currently investigating a way
of achieving RGB feeds from the
48K Spectrum.

Now onto other matters technic-
al. Earlier in the year I had a
call from one of the other local
Spectrum owners (He mainly uses
a SAM but had retained his
Spectrum). He stated that he had
had a major blow up. Normally
the term blowup is treated as an
exaggeration but in this case it
was true!...


When I investigated the situat-
ion, almost every IC within his
Spectrum, Disciple and disc
drives had its top blown off or
was cracked across the top. A
complete disaster and unfortun-
ately a complete write-off.

My assessment was that the only
thing that could case this sort
of damage was a direct connect-
ion of the 230 volt mains direct
to the Spectrums internal circ-
uits.

While I have not conclusively
proved the cause,it would appear
that a combination of a TV set
of a type without a mains trans-
former (a so called hot chassis
type) and a power extension cord


that had the phase (line) and
neutral leads transposed was the
culprit combination. The tv
set's aerial input should have
mains-rated isolating capacitors
connected in series, one of both
of these could have failed. The
extension cord was not normally
used with the computer.One some-
what positive outcome of this
episode was that it was only the
computer that was killed - it
could have just as easily been
someone's life.
                 Peter Johnson

Brian Cavers to Peter Johnson

Many thanks, Peter. I had to
split your letter into two to
fit it into OUTLETTERS so I have
put the second part in as a sep-
arate letter in OUTLETTERS 2 a
bit further on in OUTLET

                        Brian

From John Legros, BRUSSELS

Dear Ron,

Congratulations for OUTLET +D and PC - they are wonderful! I wonder if you can help me? I have a couple of questions conc- erning the Spectrum with +D...

1. What does the expression: SPECIAL FILE mean and how do you create one from BASIC?

2. What is an 'MD' file and how can one be created in BASIC?

3. How can you switch the IY machine code instruction from 23610 to another address? And for unlimited duration? -  John Legros

Brian Cavers to John Legros

The Disciple and +D SPECIAL file type is generally intended for commercial software producers. A SPECIAL file cannot be directly accessed from BASIC using LOAD and SAVE. The intention is that a commercial program would use its own machine code routines to read and write to the file thus preventing the average user from meddling with it. The file could be anything - a picture, text, program or whatever.

All files have a distinct number in the disk CAT to denote their type. A SPECIAL file is 8 so any file could be altered to a SPEC- IAL type by using SAVE @ to change the disk CAT.

The following will change the first file in the CAT to a SPEC- IAL file...

11 LOAD @1,0,1,55555 22 POKE 55555,8     :REM CAT No. 33 SAVE @1,0,1,55555

It will then show as a SPECIAL file in the CAT. The file will still load as normal, eg,a BASIC file changed to a SPECIAL in this way can still load with either LOAD P1 or LOAD d1;"NAME"

MD or M/DRIVE files will emulate microdrive files of any type. I think they were for access by machine code programs that directly access microdrives and thus would work on Disciple or *D. Their CAT code number is 6.

You should not change IY in a machine code program if it calls a ROM routine. If it doesn't and you disable interrupts with DI then there is no problem; you simply stack IY and pop it back after, eg...

DI PUSH IY                ;store IY LD IY,NNNN          ;any address program....        ;your program POP IY               ;restore IY EI RET

Alternatively you could forget the PUSH and POP and just LD IY with 23610 before exit.

When BASIC is running,IY must be ALWAYS pointing at 23610 as the offsets from that address are system variables changed by the ROM using IY. Thus in your own machine code program you can change IY permanently and leave it running all day - it doesn't matter. Only when you return to BASIC or call the ROM (probably SOME ROM routines are safe) is it crucial to restore IY to 23610.

I am assuming its necessary to disable interrupts - I've not actually looked to see if the key routines, etc. use IY.

Brian

Greetings to you and the OUTLET membership from NEW ZEALAND. It has been some time since I last contributed a letter. Although some of my technical contribut- ions have appeared over several months, these were actually written some time ago.

The following is a collection of technical bits and pieces relating to the Spectrum that I have accumulated since the original material was written. Some of it come from matters raised in the letters section and some from additional observation I have made.

What I have written about in the past has been associated with the 48K and the grey 128 +2 Spectrums. I am not able to contribute anything on the +3 as I do not have one nor any tech- nical information on this model. As far as I am aware there is only one of this type in my local area. In one letter there was a comm- ent that a green screen monitor was of low resolution (poor detail). I can assure the writer of that comment that the green screen monitor can be as sharp as a black and white one.

When using the direct video sys- tem, a green screen monitor is much superior to a colour receiver. This I can vouch for as I have three green screens monitors in regular use.

Since the material on the use of direct video for monitors was written  (see OUTLET 89,90) I have been able to obtain some RGB monitors. I knew that the RGB feed to the monitor would give a better picture display, it fact the results were excellent beyond expectations. I was able to have two monitors operating side by side for comparison. One was fed with the normal composite video, and the other with the RGB feeds, this was from a Spectrum 128 +2.

This A, B comparison immediately showed the RGB monitor to be superior in several ways. The border, paper and coloured areas were clean without any back- ground grain, text is crisp and clean without any colour fringes and the colours are clean and precise.

When one analyses the situation it stands to reason that the results would be better. Within the computer the three colour signals RED, BLUE  and GREEN (RGB) are each generated separ- ately: the monitor display tube has three separate guns to acti- vate the RED , BLUE and GREEN dots on the screen.

It seems to be a pointless extr- avagance to require a complex integrated circuit within the computer to mix (encode) the RGB signals then within the monitor to use equally complex circuit to unmix (decode) these same signals back again just to enable them to be fed between the computer and monitor via a single short piece of coaxial cable. The encoding and subse- quent decoding involve a number of compromises and as a result the picture quality suffers.

The requirements for this encoding process being used are historical.When the Spectrum and other similar computers were originally produced a normal

domestic TV set was available for the display and its input is the encoded signal. This in turn was the reqirement of the broad- casting system since only one transmitter is used to carry the tv signal.

To give some variety to this written material, load the TEST- CARD program.

[Press N to load it here now or C from the CONTENTS page - Ed]

This test chart has a number of features which can be used to check and if necessary adjust your monitor/TV set...

1  The black squares around the perimeter are true black, adjust the BRIGHTNESS control to set these to a true black and not a grey.

2  The colour bars should all be clearly defined, note that the lower third of these is BRIGHT which will show if this is available. On a black and white monitor, or if the colour can be turned off, these colour bars will show as a grey scale with the right hand blue bar appear- ing as a dark grey. The contrast control should be adjusted so each bar from left to right is a decending order of brightness.

3  The background and border should be a pure white without a green or blue or red cast Inter- nal adjustments within the moni- tor are necessary to correct a colour cast.

4  The resolution blocks across the lower centre should be clearly defined without colour fringes. The righthand one is individual pixels. These will show clearly on a good quality black and white/green monitor but will not show on a colour receiver even on direct video. A high resolution colour monitor will show these only on a RGB input.

5   The cross hatch grid lines should also be clearly defined black lines. A red ,blue,or yellow fringe on either side or above or below the lines in one or more parts of the display indicates a possible convergence error.This will require internal adjustment of the colour monitor or tv set to correct.

A blue or yellow outline on the vertical lines and also on the resolution blocks probably indi- cates an encoding error, this will only appear on a composite video feed and not on RGB inputs. Both my 128 +2 exhibit this problem which I suspect is a design defect.

6  Each colour block should finish precisely and not tend to tail off to the right.  Again, this effect sould only appear on a composite video feed and not on RGB.The likely cause is the same design defect as mentioned in 5. Should it occur on an RGB fed monitor the cause might be poor performance of the monitor video amplifiers or poor cable driver systems within the computor.

A test chart such as this can give a good indication of how well or otherwise your computer display is performing. A lot more could be said but I will leave that for now.

The 48k Spectrum can be modified to provide a a direct video feed to a monitor, a video amplifier to do this was described in an earlier issue. (OUTLET 89 and 90) However as it stands it has no facilities for RGB feeds. I am currently investigating a way of achieving RGB feeds from the 48K Spectrum.

Now onto other matters technic- al. Earlier in the year I had a call from one of the other local Spectrum owners (He mainly uses a SAM but had retained his Spectrum). He stated that he had had a major blow up. Normally the term blowup is treated as an exaggeration but in this case it was true!...

When I investigated the situat- ion, almost every IC within his Spectrum, Disciple and disc drives had its top blown off or was cracked across the top. A complete disaster and unfortun- ately a complete write-off.

My assessment was that the only thing that could case this sort of damage was a direct connect- ion of the 230 volt mains direct to the Spectrums internal circ- uits.

While I have not conclusively proved the cause,it would appear that a combination of a TV set of a type without a mains trans- former (a so called hot chassis type) and a power extension cord

that had the phase (line) and neutral leads transposed was the culprit combination. The tv set's aerial input should have mains-rated isolating capacitors connected in series, one of both of these could have failed. The extension cord was not normally used with the computer.One some- what positive outcome of this episode was that it was only the computer that was killed - it could have just as easily been someone's life. ### Brian Cavers отвечает John Legros

Тип файлов SPECIAL для Disciple и +D обычно предназначен для коммерческих производителей программного обеспечения. К файлу SPECIAL нельзя получить прямой доступ из BASIC с помощью команд LOAD и SAVE. Замысел в том, чтобы коммерческая программа использовала собственные процедуры машинного кода для чтения и записи в файл, тем самым не позволяя рядовому пользователю вмешиваться в него. Файлом может быть что угодно — картинка, текст, программа или что-то еще.

Все файлы имеют определенный номер в CAT диска для обозначения их типа. У файла SPECIAL это 8, поэтому любой файл можно изменить на тип SPECIAL, используя SAVE @ для правки каталога диска (CAT).

Следующий пример изменит первый файл в каталоге на файл SPECIAL...

```basic
11 LOAD @1,0,1,55555
22 POKE 55555,8     :REM CAT No.
33 SAVE @1,0,1,55555
```

После этого он будет отображаться в CAT как файл SPECIAL. Файл по-прежнему будет загружаться как обычно, например, файл BASIC, измененный на SPECIAL таким способом, все еще можно загрузить как с помощью `LOAD P1`, так и с помощью `LOAD d1;"NAME"`.

Файлы MD или M/DRIVE эмулируют файлы микродрайва любого типа. Думаю, они предназначались для доступа из программ на машинном коде, которые напрямую работают с микродрайвами, чтобы они могли функционировать на Disciple или +D. Их код в CAT — номер 6.

Вам не следует менять IY в программе на машинном коде, если она вызывает процедуры ROM. Если же она этого не делает и вы отключаете прерывания командой DI, то никаких проблем нет; вы просто отправляете IY в стек и забираете обратно после, например...

```text
DI
PUSH IY                ;сохранить IY
LD IY,NNNN          ;любой адрес
program....        ;ваша программа
POP IY               ;восстановить IY
EI
RET
```

Либо вы можете забыть про PUSH и POP и просто загрузить в IY значение 23610 (LD IY,23610) перед выходом.

Когда работает BASIC, IY ВСЕГДА должен указывать на 23610, поскольку смещения от этого адреса являются системными переменными, изменяемыми ROM с помощью регистра IY. Таким образом, в собственной программе на машинном коде вы можете изменить IY на постоянной основе и оставить ее работать хоть на весь день — это не имеет значения. Только когда вы возвращаетесь в BASIC или вызываете ROM (вероятно, НЕКОТОРЫЕ процедуры ROM безопасны), критически важно восстановить IY на 23610.

Я полагаю, что отключать прерывания необходимо — я сам детально не проверял, используют ли IY подпрограммы обработки клавиатуры и т.д.

Brian

Эта испытательная таблица содержит ряд элементов, которые можно использовать для проверки и, при необходимости, настройки вашего монитора/телевизора...

1. Черные квадраты по периметру — истинно черного цвета; отрегулируйте ручку BRIGHTNESS (яркость) так, чтобы они стали действительно черными, а не серыми.

2. Все цветовые полосы должны быть четко разделены; обратите внимание, что нижняя треть этих полос отображается с повышенной яркостью (BRIGHT), что позволяет проверить работу этого режима. На черно-белом мониторе (или если отключить цвет) эти полосы отобразятся в виде шкалы градаций серого, причем крайняя правая синяя полоса будет темно-серой. Регулятор контрастности следует настроить так, чтобы каждая полоса слева направо шла с убыванием яркости.

3. Фон и бордюр должны быть чисто белыми, без зеленоватого, синеватого или красноватого оттенка. Для устранения паразитного цветового оттенка потребуется внутренняя регулировка монитора.

4. Блоки проверки разрешения в нижней центральной части должны быть четко различимы и не иметь цветовых ореолов. Крайний правый блок состоит из отдельных пикселей. Они будут отчетливо видны на качественном черно-белом или зеленом мониторе, но сольются на цветном телевизоре даже при прямом видеоподключении. Цветной монитор высокого разрешения покажет их только через RGB-вход.

5. Сетка перекрестных линий (cross hatch) также должна состоять из четких черных линий. Красная, синяя или желтая окантовка с любой стороны линий на том или ином участке экрана указывает на возможную ошибку сведения лучей (convergence error). Для ее устранения потребуется внутренняя юстировка цветного монитора или телевизора.

Синий или желтый контур на вертикальных линиях, а также на блоках разрешения, скорее всего, свидетельствует об ошибке кодирования сигнала; это проявляется только при композитном подключении и напрочь отсутствует при подаче RGB. Оба моих 128 +2 страдают этой болячкой, что, как я подозреваю, является конструктивным недостатком схемотехники.

6. Каждый цветовой блок должен заканчиваться четко, без смазывания вправо. Опять же, этот эффект должен проявляться только при композитном видеосигнале, но не по RGB. Вероятная причина — тот же конструктивный дефект, о котором говорилось в пункте 5. Если же такое происходит на мониторе с RGB-входом, причиной может быть плохая работа видеоусилителей монитора или плохая схема буферизации кабеля внутри компьютера.

Подобная тестовая таблица дает хорошее представление о том, насколько качественно или плохо работает дисплей вашего компьютера. Можно было бы сказать еще многое, но пока я остановлюсь на этом.

Spectrum 48K можно модифицировать для прямого вывода видеосигнала на монитор — видеоусилитель для этой цели описывался в предыдущих номерах (OUTLET 89 и 90). Однако в исходном виде он не имеет возможности вывода RGB. В настоящее время я исследую способ получения RGB-сигнала со Spectrum 48K.

Теперь к другим техническим вопросам. Ранее в этом году мне позвонил один из местных владельцев Spectrum (в основном он пользуется SAM, но сохранил и свой Spectrum). Он заявил, что у него произошел серьезный взрыв. Обычно слово «взрыв» воспринимается как преувеличение, но в данном случае это была чистая правда!..

Когда я осмотрел аппаратуру, то обнаружил, что почти у каждой микросхемы внутри его Spectrum, Disciple и дисководов оторвало верхнюю часть корпуса или она треснула пополам. Полнейшая катастрофа и, к сожалению, полное списание оборудования.

По моей оценке, единственное, что могло вызвать подобные повреждения — это прямое попадание сетевого напряжения 230 вольт во внутренние цепи Spectrum.

Хотя я и не доказал причину на все сто процентов, судя по всему, виной стало сочетание телевизора без сетевого трансформатора (так называемое «горячее шасси») и сетевого удлинителя, в котором фазный и нулевой провода были перепутаны местами. В антенном входе телевизора должны быть последовательно включены высоковольтные разделительные конденсаторы — один из них или оба могли пробиться. Этот удлинитель обычно с компьютером не использовался. Единственным утешительным итогом этого происшествия стало то, что погиб только компьютер — с таким же успехом это могла быть чья-то жизнь.
